headline: Scientists Engineer Yeast to Turn Plastic Waste Into Edible Cookies
meta_description: NASA-backed researchers at Southern Illinois University have engineered yeast to convert plastic waste and agricultural leftovers into protein-rich 3D-printed…
summary_short: Researchers have engineered yeast to transform plastic bottles and farm waste into edible proteins and vitamins for 3D-printed cookies that could feed people in space.
body:
Scientists at Southern Illinois University have engineered yeast to perform an unlikely transformation: converting plastic waste and agricultural leftovers into edible proteins, vitamins, and flavorings. The result is a protein-rich cookie called µBites (microbites), created through 3D printing and developed partly for NASA's Deep Space Food Challenge. The breakthrough addresses two pressing global problems at once—plastic pollution and food insecurity—while creating a potential food source for environments where conventional supplies cannot reach, from disaster zones on Earth to future human settlements on the Moon or Mars.

The process begins with oxidative hydrothermal dissolution, a proprietary technique developed by SIU Carbondale Geology Professor Ken Anderson that breaks down resistant materials like PET plastic (found in soda and water bottles) and discarded corn stalks using water and oxygen under high temperature and pressure. The resulting smaller molecules are then fed to engineered yeast strains, including baker's yeast, which transform them into new food components. One strain now produces vanilla flavoring from plant biomass; another generates beta carotene from PET-derived ethylene glycol, which the body converts into vitamin A.

Though institutional approval is still pending for formal taste tests, preliminary evaluations based on aroma have been promising. When asked about eating µBites in resource-scarce situations, most participants said they would be willing. The research team is working to make the cookies more appealing for everyday consumption and hopes to have them ready for public use within the next few years. Their ultimate goal is to have microbes produce even more ingredients—including starch, fiber, and sweetener—moving from waste problem to food solution.
quick_facts: Engineered yeast converts PET plastic and agricultural waste into food ingredients
Southern Illinois University team developed the technology for NASA's Deep Space Food Challenge
3D-printed cookies called µBites contain proteins, vitamins, and engineered vanilla flavoring
Process uses oxidative hydrothermal dissolution to break down resistant plastics and biomass
Scientists hope µBites could be ready for public consumption within a few years
